seeds.goal: You can write a balanced essay: present the strongest arguments on both sides with evidence and reach a conclusion that follows from them.

seeds.task: Write a for-and-against essay (220–260 words) on whether university lectures should move online: an introduction that frames the question, two arguments for, two against, and a conclusion that follows from the evidence.
model: Frame the question without answering it
Since 2020, most universities have kept at least part of their teaching online, and the debate has moved from whether it is possible to whether it is better.
The clearest advantage is access: a student in a small town can now attend a course that used to require moving to the capital and paying rent for four years.
Furthermore, recorded lectures allow students to stop, rewind and re-watch, which is particularly valuable for those studying in a second language.
On the other hand, several studies report a sharp fall in participation: in one survey of 4,000 students, the proportion asking questions dropped from 34 to 9 per cent once cameras were optional.
In addition, online teaching removes what happens after the lecture — the corridor conversation where most misunderstandings are actually repaired.
The two sets of arguments are not symmetrical: access is a structural gain, whereas the loss of interaction is a design problem that can be reduced.
Conclude in line with the evidence
On balance, lectures can reasonably move online provided that seminars stay in the room, since it is the seminar, not the lecture, that depends on people looking at each other.
The question is not online or offline, but which part of teaching each format is actually good at.

seeds.task: Write an opinion essay (220–260 words) on whether national museums should be free: state your thesis, give two distinct supporting arguments with evidence, concede the strongest counter-argument, answer it, and conclude without weakening.
model: State the thesis in the first paragraph
National museums should be free at the point of entry, and the cost should be met from the same budget that maintains the buildings.
The first reason is behavioural: a paid ticket turns a museum into an event, and an event is something you do once, whereas free entry turns it into a habit.
When British national museums removed charges in 2001, visits rose by roughly 70 per cent within four years, and the largest increase came from first-time visitors.
The second reason is that entry fees do not fund museums; they fund the collection of entry fees.
In several mid-sized institutions ticketing staff, systems and security absorb a substantial share of the income the tickets produce.
Admittedly, free entry shifts the cost onto taxpayers who may never visit, and that objection cannot be dismissed as unfair.
However, the same argument applies to public libraries and street lighting: we fund them because their value is not confined to the people who use them on a given day.
A museum that charges protects its budget and loses its public. The trade is not worth making, and the decision should be made once rather than reopened every time a budget is tight.

The purpose of this report is to establish how the library is used outside teaching hours and to recommend changes to opening times.
Entry data for eight weeks were analysed and a questionnaire was completed by 316 students; twelve students were interviewed individually.
First, use is highly concentrated: 61 per cent of all entries occur between 17:00 and 21:00, while the morning hours account for 12 per cent.

model: This proposal recommends the introduction of a peer-tutoring scheme in mathematics for classes 8 and 9.
In the last two terms, 38 students in these year groups received a failing grade in at least one mathematics test, and the same eleven names appear in both terms.

seeds.goal: You can review a work analytically: describe what it attempts, judge how well it succeeds with evidence, compare it and name its audience.
seeds.why: An analytical review does not ask 'did I like it' but 'what was it trying to do, and did it do that'. The shift is what separates B2 from B1.

seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: by what standard does the reviewer judge the film?
seeds.task: Write an analytical review (200–240 words) of a film, book or exhibition: what it attempts, how it works, one strength and one weakness with evidence, a comparison, its audience and a verdict.
model: Name the work and its aim
The documentary 'Fifty Metres' sets out to show what a single street in Almaty looks like across one year.
It is built from one fixed camera position and roughly four hundred hours of footage, cut down to eighty minutes without commentary.
Its greatest achievement is patience: the sequence in which a kiosk is dismantled over three weeks turns an ordinary economic fact into something you cannot look away from.
The absence of narration forces the viewer to read the street the way its residents do, from repetition and small changes rather than from explanation.
The film is less successful when it abandons its own rule: three short interviews in the final quarter explain what the previous hour had already shown.
Compared with the observational documentaries it clearly admires, it is more generous to its subjects and less interested in irony.
It will reward viewers who are prepared to watch a street rather than a story, and will frustrate anyone expecting a thesis about the city.
Judged by its own aim — to make an ordinary place visible — it succeeds, and the three interviews are the only evidence that its makers doubted it would.

Если судить по его собственной цели, …
… the only evidence that its makers doubted it.

seeds.task: Write a problem-solution essay (220–260 words) about food waste in cities: define the problem precisely with data, identify two causes, propose two solutions, evaluate their cost and effectiveness, and conclude.
model: Roughly a third of the food produced for cities is thrown away, but the losses are not evenly distributed: most of them happen in the last two stages, in shops and in households.
In a city the size of Almaty this represents several hundred tonnes a day, most of it edible at the moment it is discarded.
The first cause is the date system: 'best before' and 'use by' are treated as identical by consumers, although only one of them concerns safety.
The second, which most campaigns ignore, is portion and package size: a household of one buys bread designed for a household of four.
The clearest first measure is regulatory rather than educational: standardising date labels and requiring shops to display the difference at the shelf, not on the packet.
The second is to make small formats economically rational, since single portions are currently priced at a premium that pushes buyers towards packs they cannot finish.
The first measure costs almost nothing and has been shown to reduce discards by around a tenth; the second requires pressure on producers and will take years.

Neither measure solves the problem, and campaigns urging people to plan their shopping have already been tried at scale without measurable effect. Structural changes are slower, but they are the only ones that survive the week they are announced.

seeds.goal: You can compare two options systematically: choose criteria, apply each to both options, and reach a recommendation for a defined situation.
seeds.why: Weak comparisons describe A and then describe B. Strong ones move criterion by criterion, which is the only way the reader can decide.

seeds.task: Write a comparison essay (220–260 words) comparing two ways of learning a language — an intensive course abroad and a year of weekly classes at home: choose three criteria, compare both on each, and recommend one for a specific learner.
model: For a learner with a fixed budget and one year available, an intensive month abroad and a year of weekly classes at home are the two realistic options, and they differ on three criteria that matter.
The first is exposure. A month abroad provides perhaps 300 hours of contact; a year of two-hour weekly classes provides around 80, although homework narrows the gap slightly.

The second is retention, and here the ranking reverses: skills acquired intensively decay quickly without maintenance, while weekly classes distribute practice across months, which is the pattern memory research consistently favours.

The third is cost per hour of speaking. The course abroad is far more expensive in total, but its cost per hour of actual speech is often lower, since a class of twelve at home gives each student a few minutes per lesson.
These criteria interact: the intensive option produces a level that the weekly option would take two years to reach, but only if something maintains it afterwards.
For a learner who has a specific deadline — an examination or a job — the intensive month is the better investment.
For a learner with no deadline and no way to continue speaking afterwards, weekly classes will produce more usable language in the same year.
The deciding variable is not the teaching but what happens in the eleven months nobody plans for.

seeds.goal: You can summarise a text accurately and then respond to it: separate what the author said from what you think, and answer the argument rather than the topic.
seeds.why: This is the core academic skill: most weak essays argue with a position the author never held.

seeds.read: Read the text and find one thing: where does the summary end and the comment begin?
seeds.task: Write a summary and comment (200–240 words) on an article claiming that homework should be abolished: summarise the argument fairly in one paragraph, then respond — agree with something, dispute something, and add something the article missed.
model: Name the text and its claim
In 'The homework illusion', the author argues that homework before the age of fourteen has no measurable effect on attainment and should be abolished.

Her case rests on two pillars: a meta-analysis showing negligible correlation in primary education, and the observation that homework transfers teaching to parents whose ability to help is unequally distributed.
She concedes that reading at home is an exception and that the picture changes in secondary school.
The second pillar is the stronger one, and it is under-used: an exercise that a graduate parent can explain in five minutes may be impossible in a household where nobody can.

The first pillar is weaker than it appears, since the studies aggregated measure attainment in tests taken at the end of the same year, which is precisely the timescale over which distributed practice shows least benefit.
The article also omits what replaces homework: in the two systems that abolished it, the school day lengthened by roughly forty minutes, which is a different reform with different costs.
The reasonable conclusion is narrower than the author's: homework that requires adult explanation should be abolished; homework that requires only time should not.
The distinction is easy to state and would survive contact with a real timetable, which is more than can be said for abolition.

seeds.goal: You can report survey results: describe the sample, present the main figures in words, identify a pattern and state what the data cannot show.
seeds.why: Reporting data is where most writers overclaim. Naming the limits of your own survey is what makes the rest believable.
seeds.ex: Bekzat's report stated its own margin of error. It was the only student report the department cited.
seeds.read: Read the report and find one thing: what does the writer say the data cannot show?
seeds.task: Write a survey report (200–240 words) on students' reading habits: aim, sample and method, three findings in words rather than tables, one pattern, one limitation and a conclusion.
model: This report presents the results of a survey into the reading habits of students in years 10 and 11.
The questionnaire was completed online by 248 of 402 students, a response rate of 62 per cent, over two weeks in October.
Almost two thirds of respondents reported reading something outside school every day, but only 14 per cent were reading a book at the time of the survey.
Of those who were reading a book, three quarters had chosen it themselves rather than being set it, and their reported enjoyment was more than twice as high.
Time was named as the main obstacle by 71 per cent, well ahead of interest, which was named by 19 per cent.
Taken together, the figures suggest a population that reads constantly in short pieces and rarely at length, which is a difference of format rather than of appetite.
The data cannot show whether the pattern is new: no comparable survey was carried out in this school before 2023, and self-reported reading time is generally overstated.
Any measure aimed at 'making students read' would therefore be aimed at the wrong target; measures aimed at protecting long blocks of time have a better claim on the evidence.

seeds.goal: You can write about a technology for a general audience: explain what it does in plain language, give one concrete use, name the trade-off and judge it.
seeds.why: Technology writing fails in two ways: unexplained jargon, or enthusiasm with no cost attached. The genre demands both clarity and scepticism.
seeds.ex: Miras explained machine translation for a school magazine, including what it cannot do. Two language teachers asked to reprint it.
seeds.read: Read the article and find one thing: what does the writer say the technology cannot do?
seeds.task: Write an article (200–240 words) explaining a technology to a general reader: what problem it solves, how it works in plain language, one concrete example, its limits, the trade-off and a judgement.
model: Machine translation solves a problem that used to require a person: turning text in one language into usable text in another, immediately and at no cost.
Modern systems do not translate word by word; they are trained on millions of pairs of sentences and predict, for each fragment, what a translator would most probably have written.
This explains both its fluency and its failures: the output is always plausible, whether or not it is right.
Ask it to translate a legal clause with 'shall' and it will produce something that reads perfectly and may reverse the obligation.
It has no access to the situation: it cannot know whether 'you' is one person or a room, formal or intimate, and in Kazakh or Russian that decision is unavoidable.
The trade-off is speed against verification: the time saved is real, but it moves the work from translating to checking, which requires exactly the knowledge the tool was supposed to replace.
Say where it is right to use it
For understanding a text, it is now better than most learners; for producing a text somebody will act on, it is a first draft and nothing more.
The technology is neither the end of language learning nor a toy. It removes the easy half of translation and leaves the half that was always difficult.

seeds.goal: You can argue an education question: define the terms, use evidence rather than experience, address the strongest counter-position and conclude precisely.
seeds.why: Education essays attract personal anecdote. At B2 the marks go to the writer who argues from evidence and defines what they mean.
seeds.ex: Dana's essay defined 'streaming' in the first paragraph. Her teacher said it was the reason the rest held together.
seeds.read: Read the essay and find one thing: how does the writer define the key term?
seeds.task: Write an essay (220–260 words) on whether students should be grouped by ability: define the practice, give the case for, the case against with evidence, address the strongest objection and conclude.
model: By ability grouping I mean the practice of teaching the same subject to separate classes based on prior attainment, not the temporary grouping that happens inside a lesson.
The argument for it is intuitive; the evidence for it is weaker than most people assume.
The case for is that a teacher facing a narrower range can pitch the lesson accurately, and that the strongest students are not held to the pace of the class.
However, large-scale reviews consistently find negligible average effects, with a pattern hidden inside that average: modest gains for the top group and measurable losses for the bottom one.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Lower groups are more often taught by less experienced staff, are given a narrower curriculum, and are told, in every way except words, what has been decided about them.
The strongest objection to abolishing it is practical: mixed classes are harder to teach, and a policy that assumes an excellent teacher in every room is a policy about an imaginary school.
That objection argues for investment in teaching, not for a structure whose measured cost falls on the students with the least.
Ability grouping should be used where it is temporary, subject-specific and reversible, and abandoned where it decides at eleven what will be taught at sixteen.

seeds.goal: You can write about an environmental question: quantify the problem, distinguish measures by scale, address cost and distribution, and conclude.
seeds.why: Environmental writing drowns in good intentions. The marks are in the numbers and in the honest question of who pays.
seeds.ex: Sanzhar's essay compared the effect of two measures by tonnes rather than by feeling. It was read out to his class.
seeds.read: Read the essay and find one thing: which measure does the writer say is over-valued?
seeds.task: Write an essay (220–260 words) on what individuals can realistically do about climate change: quantify the problem, compare two individual measures by scale, address the objection about corporate responsibility, and conclude.
model: Individual action on climate is worth discussing only in terms of scale: the question is not whether an action is good, but how much of the problem it reaches.
An average household in a country like Kazakhstan is responsible for the order of ten tonnes of CO2 a year, of which heating and transport account for the majority.
Recycling, the measure most people name first, addresses a small fraction of that total, and the fraction is smaller still where the sorting infrastructure is incomplete.
Insulating a flat, by contrast, reduces the largest single line in the household total, and it does so every year rather than once.
The comparison is not close: the two measures differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and only one of them is normally described as an effort.
The standard objection is that individual measures are a distraction, since a hundred companies account for the majority of emissions.

The objection is right about attribution and wrong about consequence: those emissions are produced to heat the flats and move the people who make individual decisions, and the political will to regulate producers has never appeared in a population that has changed nothing itself.
The reasonable position is therefore neither guilt nor dismissal: choose the two decisions in a household that are measured in tonnes, and treat the rest as hygiene rather than as policy.

seeds.goal: You can write a case study: describe the situation, the intervention, the result with data, and what transfers to other cases.
seeds.why: A case study is only useful if the reader can tell whether their situation is similar. That judgement lives in the details you choose.
seeds.ex: Aigerim wrote up a reading project in one page. Two other schools ran it from her description alone.
seeds.read: Read the case study and find one thing: what does the writer say would not transfer to another school?
seeds.task: Write a case study (200–240 words) of something that was tried and worked: the situation with numbers, what was done, the result with data, what caused it, and what would and would not transfer elsewhere.
model: In September 2023, 41 of 96 students in years 5 and 6 were reading below the expected level, and the school library was issuing fewer than twenty books a week.
There was no budget for new books and no free hour in the timetable.
The intervention was narrow: the first fifteen minutes of Tuesday's and Thursday's second lesson were given to silent reading, in every subject, with the teacher reading as well.
The detail that mattered was the last part: in the two classes where the teacher marked work instead of reading, the effect disappeared entirely.
After two terms, library issues had risen from under twenty to about ninety a week, and 28 of the 41 students had moved up at least one band in the school's own assessment.
The measure cost nothing except thirty minutes of teaching time a week.
What transfers is the mechanism: protected time, no assessment attached, and an adult visibly doing the same thing.

What does not transfer is the starting point: this school already had a library within the building, and in a school where books have to be requested a week in advance the same fifteen minutes would produce nothing.

seeds.goal: You can escalate a complaint: summarise what has happened, quote what you were told, explain why the answer is inadequate and state the next step you will take.
seeds.why: Escalation letters work when they are unemotional and precise. Anger reads as weakness; a chronology reads as a threat.

Your reply states that 'the transaction was completed successfully on our side' and that I should contact the receiving bank.

In the meantime, I have paid a penalty of 12,000 tenge on the payment this transfer was intended to make, and I have spent four working days on telephone queues.
I therefore repeat my request: the return of 180,000 tenge, compensation of the 12,000 penalty, and a written explanation of where the transfer was held.

seeds.goal: You can write a report that ends in a decision: state the decision to be made, the options, the criteria, how each option scores and your recommendation.
seeds.why: This genre is what management actually reads. A recommendation without visible criteria is an opinion in a suit.
seeds.ex: Aisultan's report chose between two suppliers on four stated criteria. The committee accepted it without discussion.

model: State the decision to be made
This report recommends which platform the school should adopt for online homework from September.
Three options were considered: continuing with the current system, moving to Platform A, and moving to Platform B.
The options were assessed against four criteria: cost over three years, teacher training time, offline access for students, and the ability to export data if we leave.
The current system is cheapest and requires no training, but it has no offline mode, which affects the 14 per cent of students who reported unstable internet in the March survey.
Platform A performs best on offline access and costs 40 per cent more; its training requirement is one afternoon per teacher.
Platform B is the most capable and the most expensive, and it exports data only in its own format, which makes leaving it expensive in a way that is easy to underestimate.

Platform A is recommended. The deciding criterion is offline access: it is the only criterion on which the current system fails a group of students rather than an administrator.

seeds.goal: You can write a reflective account: describe an experience honestly, analyse what happened and why, and say what you will do differently.
seeds.why: Reflection without a change is a diary entry. Universities and employers read this genre for the last paragraph.
seeds.ex: Kamila wrote about a failed group project without blaming anyone. Her tutor called it the most useful text in the portfolio.
seeds.read: Read the account and find one thing: what will the writer do differently next time?
seeds.task: Write a reflective account (200–240 words) of something that did not go well: what happened, your role in it, what you now think caused it, what you learned and one specific change you will make.
model: Last term I led a group project on water quality with four classmates, and we submitted it eleven days late and incomplete.
My part in that was not the workload; it was that I allocated tasks in a group chat and never checked whether anybody had started.
Three days before the deadline I discovered that two of the four sections existed only as a title, and both people believed the other one was writing them.
I rewrote both sections myself in two evenings, which saved the submission and taught everybody involved the wrong lesson.
Looking back, the cause was a confusion between agreeing and committing: everybody agreed in the chat, and nobody said a date out loud.
I also avoided asking directly because a check felt like an accusation, which is exactly the assumption that makes a group fail quietly rather than loudly.
What I learned is that a check is a form of respect, and that the discomfort of asking on day three is a fraction of the discomfort of finding out on day eleven.
In the current project I have introduced one rule: every task has a named person and a date, and on that date the person sends what exists, even if it is two paragraphs.

seeds.goal: You can explore a question in public writing: open with a concrete case, examine two readings of it, resist the easy conclusion and end where the evidence leaves you.
seeds.why: Blog writing tempts you into certainty. The posts people return to are the ones that admit what they do not know.
seeds.ex: Aliya's post about scoring systems in schools was quoted in a teachers' newsletter for its final paragraph.
seeds.read: Read the post and find one thing: what does the writer refuse to conclude?
seeds.task: Write a discursive blog post (200–240 words): start with a concrete case, give two competing readings of it, weigh them, refuse the easy conclusion and end honestly.
model: Our school replaced marks with written comments for one term in year 7, and then quietly brought the marks back.
What is interesting is not the reversal but who asked for it: not the teachers, and not the administration, but the students themselves.
One reading is that marks are motivating, and that removing them removed the only reason a large part of the class did the work at all.
Another is that comments took three days to arrive, and a student who cannot tell whether the work was good until Thursday will take the number that arrives on Monday.
The second reading fits our own data better: in the two classes where comments were returned the next day, nobody asked for marks back.
But that comparison involves two teachers who volunteered, which is exactly the group most likely to produce a good result whatever the system.
So I cannot say that comments work and marks do not. What the term showed is narrower: feedback that arrives late is worse than a number, and that is a fact about speed, not about numbers.
End where the evidence leaves you

The interesting experiment would be comments returned within a day, at scale, for a year. Nobody has run it here, and until somebody does, the argument is about principles rather than about our students.

seeds.goal: You can review a book: place it, describe its argument or story, judge its execution with quotation, compare it and say who should read it.
seeds.why: The commonest failure in reviews is reviewing the book you wanted. The discipline is judging what is actually on the page.

seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: what does the reviewer say the book does not do?

model: 'The Silk Road: A New History' arrives in a crowded field: at least four popular histories of the same subject have appeared in the last decade.
Its distinguishing claim is that the road was never a road, and that treating it as one has produced two centuries of misleading maps.
The author builds the case from customs records rather than from travellers' accounts, which is the book's most valuable decision.
The chapter on silver is the strongest: 'a merchant in Merv knew the price in Chang'an the way a farmer knows the weather — indirectly, late, and well enough to act.'
That sentence does what the whole book does best: it converts an abstraction about networks into something a reader can picture.
What the book does not do is explain how the system ended. The final chapter covers four centuries in twenty pages and reaches for plague and politics without choosing between them.
Compared with Frankopan's account, it is narrower, better evidenced and considerably less exciting.
It suits readers who already know the outline and want the mechanism; a reader coming to the subject for the first time will find the first eighty pages assume a map they do not have.

seeds.goal: You can evaluate a project: restate its aims, measure the outcome against them, separate what worked from what was lucky, and recommend.
seeds.why: Evaluation is where projects get their honesty. The test is whether you would reach the same conclusion if the result had been bad.
seeds.ex: Miras evaluated a school recycling scheme and recommended stopping it. The committee agreed and reused the budget.
seeds.read: Read the evaluation and find one thing: which aim was not met?
seeds.task: Write a project evaluation (200–240 words): the aims as stated, what was done, results against each aim, what the results do not prove, and a recommendation.
model: This evaluation covers the paper-recycling scheme run in the school between September and May.
Restate the aims as they were stated
The scheme had two stated aims: to reduce the volume of paper sent to general waste by half, and to raise 150,000 tenge for the library through the sale of collected paper.
Bins were placed on three floors, two classes took responsibility for emptying them, and collection was arranged fortnightly with a local company.
Give the result against the first aim
The first aim was met: measured over four weeks in April, general waste contained 46 per cent less paper by weight than in the same weeks a year earlier.
Give the result against the second aim
The second was not: the scheme raised 31,000 tenge, because the price paid for mixed paper fell by two thirds during the year.
It should be noted that the reduction coincided with the move of two departments to digital worksheets, which was decided independently and may account for a substantial part of it.
The scheme required about forty hours of student time and a small storage room that was otherwise unused.

It is recommended that the collection continue, but that the fundraising aim be dropped rather than restated: a scheme justified by income will be judged on income, and this one cannot compete with the paper price.

seeds.goal: You can apologise on behalf of a group: state what happened, accept responsibility without naming individuals, describe the remedy and the change, and avoid the passive-voice evasion.

model: To everyone who registered for the winter conference,
We cancelled the conference nineteen hours before it was due to begin, and we told you by a single message at 21:40.
The decision was ours and the delay in announcing it was ours: we had known since Thursday morning that the venue could not confirm, and we waited for a confirmation that we had no reason to expect.
Forty-one of you had already travelled, and eleven had paid for accommodation that could not be refunded.
We will refund all registration fees this week without a request, and we will reimburse documented accommodation costs on presentation of a receipt, up to 25,000 tenge.
We have also changed the rule that caused this: from now on, if a venue is unconfirmed 72 hours before an event, we announce the risk immediately rather than waiting for certainty.
We are not going to describe this as a venue problem. The venue was unreliable; the decision to keep that from you was ours.
The conference will run on 14 March in a confirmed venue, and everyone registered keeps their place. Aigerim Serik, on behalf of the organising committee.

seeds.goal: You can analyse a film: identify what it does to the viewer and show, with specific scenes, the techniques that produce the effect.
seeds.why: Analysis is not opinion with longer sentences. The test is whether you name a technique and connect it to an effect.
seeds.ex: Dana's analysis of a single scene was used in class to teach the difference between review and analysis.
seeds.read: Read the analysis and find one thing: which technique does the writer connect to the film's tension?
seeds.task: Write a film analysis (200–240 words): the effect the film produces, two techniques that produce it with specific scenes, one place where the technique fails, and a conclusion about the film's method.
model: State the effect and the claim
'The Return' produces its tension almost entirely without music, and it does so through two decisions that are visible in the first ten minutes.
Name the first technique with a scene
The first is duration: the scene in which the two brothers wait in the car lasts four minutes and contains no dialogue after the first line.
Because the audience knows the father is inside the house and does not know why, the length itself becomes the source of dread; nothing is added except time.
The second is camera position: the father is filmed from below in every scene until the boat sequence, and from above afterwards.
The shift is never remarked on, and it arrives exactly at the point where the older brother stops obeying — the film gives the viewer the information visually before the plot delivers it.
The technique fails once: the storm sequence uses music for ninety seconds, and the scene is the least frightening in the film, precisely because the score tells the audience what to feel.
Compared with the conventional thriller, which signals danger in advance, this film withholds signals and lets the viewer supply them.
The method is consistent: every time the film explains itself, it loses the tension it built by refusing to.

connItems.a: Some argue that fines change behaviour.
connItems.b: , the evidence from Norway suggests otherwise.
connItems.why: You answer a claim by naming the counter-evidence.

connItems.a: The proposal is ambitious and well argued.
connItems.b: , it depends on funding that does not yet exist.
connItems.why: A balanced judgement gives both halves.

connItems.a: Working from home suits experienced staff.
connItems.b: , it isolates those who have just joined.
connItems.why: In contrast separates two groups with opposite outcomes.

connItems.a: The company cut its prices twice.
connItems.b: , its market share continued to fall.

tr.src: Lots of people think exams are bad.
ans: It is widely believed that examinations are harmful.
tr.why: Academic writing avoids 'lots of' and prefers impersonal openings.

tr.src: Cars pollute the air. They are still necessary in rural areas.
ans: While cars pollute the air, they remain necessary in rural areas.
tr.why: While packs a concession and a claim into one sentence.

tr.src: The government decided to close the plant. This caused protests.
ans: The government's decision to close the plant caused protests.
tr.why: Turning a verb into a noun tightens academic prose.

tr.cue: Use the passive to keep it impersonal
tr.src: We collected the data in March.
ans: The data was collected in March.
The data were collected in March.
tr.why: Reports keep the researcher out of the sentence.

ans: Social media may reduce concentration in some users.
tr.why: An unhedged claim is easy to refute; a hedged one is defensible.

tr.src: The team trained hard. They lost the final.
ans: Despite their hard training, the team lost the final.
tr.why: Despite takes a noun phrase; although takes a clause.

tr.src: The library is closed at weekends and students complain.
ans: The library should open at weekends.
tr.why: A report ends in recommendations, not in complaints.

tr.src: Small firms hire quickly. Large firms take months.
ans: Small firms hire within days, whereas large firms take months.
tr.why: Whereas is the cleanest way to hold two facts side by side.

ans: As prices rose by 12 per cent, sales fell accordingly.
Prices rose by 12 per cent; consequently, sales fell.
tr.why: A figure turns a claim into evidence.

tr.src: Everybody agrees that homework is useless.
ans: Many teachers now question the value of homework.
tr.why: Absolute statements collapse under a single counter-example.

tr.src: So the plan did not work.
ans: Consequently, the plan failed to achieve its aim.
tr.why: So belongs to speech; consequently belongs to a report.

tr.src: The survey covered 400 students. It was carried out online. The results were clear.
ans: The online survey of 400 students produced clear results.
tr.why: Three thin sentences make one strong one.

reg.fm: There are two arguments against this position.
reg.inf: I've got two things against this.
reg.why: Essays use impersonal structures, not chatty verbs.

reg.fm: The findings suggest that demand has fallen.
reg.inf: It looks like nobody wants it any more.
reg.why: Reports report; they do not guess out loud.

reg.ctx: A message to a colleague you know well
reg.fm: I should be most grateful for your assistance.
reg.inf: Could you help me with this?
reg.why: Extreme formality between colleagues creates distance you do not want.

reg.fm: This measure would reduce costs by 15 per cent.
reg.inf: This would save us a ton of money.
reg.why: A proposal needs a figure, not an impression.

reg.fm: The second half loses the tension of the first.
reg.inf: The second half was kinda boring tbh.
reg.why: Reviews are judgements, and judgements need precise language.

reg.fm: I am writing with regard to your advertisement of 4 March.
reg.inf: I saw your ad and I'm interested.
reg.why: A formal letter opens with the reference, not with your feelings.

reg.ctx: A comment in a study group chat
reg.fm: I would like to draw your attention to the deadline.
reg.why: In a chat, a plain reminder is more useful than a formula.

reg.fm: On balance, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks.
reg.inf: So all in all it's a good thing I guess.
reg.why: A conclusion must sound decided, not hesitant.

reg.fm: The service fell short of the standard advertised.
reg.inf: The service was nowhere near what you promised.
reg.why: Understatement is stronger than exaggeration in formal writing.

reg.ctx: An email to a close friend
reg.fm: I trust this message finds you well.
reg.why: The formula belongs to business email, not to friendship.

reg.ctx: A report for the school council
reg.fm: Three quarters of respondents supported the change.
reg.inf: Almost everybody was fine with it.
reg.why: A report gives the proportion, not an impression of it.

reg.fm: We recommend introducing the scheme in September.
reg.inf: Maybe we could try it in September or something.
reg.why: A recommendation that hedges itself will not be adopted.

imp.sent: The report shows a big rise in prices.
opts: Loses the direction of the movement.
imp.why: Data language has fixed collocations: sharp increase, steady decline.

imp.sent: This idea is very bad for small businesses.
opts: One precise adjective with a clear direction.
A different claim: unpopular is not the same as harmful.
imp.why: Precision is what separates B2 from B1 vocabulary.

imp.sent: A lot of people say the policy failed.
opts: Names the group and the speech act.
An absolute claim you cannot support.
imp.why: Attribute the claim to a definable group, or do not attribute it at all.

imp.sent: The plan is good because it saves money.
opts: One word that carries the reason inside it.
Cheap is about price, not about value.
imp.why: Choose the adjective that already contains your argument.

imp.sent: The article talks about climate change.
opts: The verb of an academic text.
imp.why: Verbs of analysis are the backbone of academic register.

imp.sent: The film has a lot of good things in it.
imp.why: In reviews, abstract nouns carry the judgement.

imp.sent: The company made the situation worse.
opts: One verb instead of three words.
imp.why: Single strong verbs make formal prose dense.

imp.sent: I think the government should do something about it.
opts: A concrete measure you can defend.
imp.why: A recommendation is only useful if it names the action.

imp.sent: The results were not very clear.
opts: The exact term for results that decide nothing.
A different and much stronger claim.
imp.why: Academic English has one word for most 'not very + adjective' pairs.

imp.sent: Many young people have money problems.
opts: Neutral register for a serious topic.
imp.why: Register consistency matters more than variety.

imp.sent: The evidence in the study is not strong.
opts: Judges the authors, not the evidence.
imp.why: Criticise the evidence in the vocabulary of the field.

imp.sent: This will help the city a lot.
imp.why: Adverbs of degree replace 'a lot' in formal writing.

tl.long: It is a well-known fact that a lot of people in the modern world of today use social media every single day.
tl.model: Most people now use social media daily.
tl.why: 'It is a well-known fact' and 'the modern world of today' are pure padding.

tl.long: The purpose of this report is to give information about what the students think about the canteen.
tl.model: This report presents students' views on the canteen.
tl.why: One verb, present, replaces 'the purpose is to give information about'.

tl.long: In spite of the fact that the scheme was expensive, it was implemented by the council last year.
tl.model: Despite its cost, the council implemented the scheme last year.
tl.why: 'In spite of the fact that' is five words for despite.

tl.long: There are a number of different reasons which can explain why the sales figures went down.
tl.model: Several factors explain the fall in sales.
tl.why: 'A number of different reasons which can explain why' collapses to one noun.

tl.long: It should be pointed out that the results of the survey were not very conclusive at all.
tl.why: If a point matters, make it — do not announce that you will.

tl.long: The company has taken the decision to make a reduction in the number of its employees.
tl.model: The company has decided to cut staff numbers.
tl.why: 'Take the decision to make a reduction' hides two verbs inside nouns.

tl.long: Due to the fact that the deadline was moved, the team was able to finish the work properly.
tl.model: Because the deadline moved, the team finished the work properly.
tl.why: 'Due to the fact that' is always just because.

tl.long: At this moment in time we are not in a position to give an answer to your question.
tl.model: We cannot answer your question yet.
tl.why: Business padding: five words become one verb.

tl.long: The film is a film which tries to ask questions about what freedom really means today.
tl.model: The film questions what freedom means today.
tl.why: 'A film which tries to ask questions about' is a loop plus a hedge.

tl.long: In my own personal opinion I would say that the second proposal is the better one of the two.
tl.model: The second proposal is clearly the better one.
tl.why: Three hedges in a row cancel your own position.

rubric.task: Does the text answer the exact question asked, with a position held from start to finish?
rubric.organisation: Four paragraphs with a visible logic: claim, evidence, counter-argument, conclusion.
rubric.vocabulary: Precise, register-consistent language: collocations, not synonyms picked at random.
rubric.grammar: Complex sentences, hedging, passive and nominalisation used deliberately.
